summary: Marvell agrees to buy Lumentum for $115 billion, while papers cover latent reasoning for image generation, hierarchical world-model planning, a trained 4B robot coding agent, a multivariate forecasting foundation model, and cross-model KV-cache transfer.

news.title: Marvell agrees to buy optical-chip maker Lumentum in a $115 billion all-stock deal
news.tldr: Marvell will acquire laser and optical-module maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion, a bet that AI data centers are moving from copper to integrated optical connectivity.
news.why_selected: One of the largest chip-sector deals on record, driven directly by AI data-center networking, announced by both companies in a primary press release.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Training and serving frontier models means linking thousands of accelerators, and the wiring between them is becoming a bottleneck. Marvell designs electrical and optical interconnect chips, network switches and custom accelerators for cloud customers. Lumentum, based in San Jose, makes high-performance lasers, optical transceivers and optical circuit switches, and runs specialized compound-semiconductor factories, including indium phosphide processes. Talk of a deal began after October 28.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: On November 2, Marvell and Lumentum announced a definitive agreement for Marvell to acquire Lumentum. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.500 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share, which implies about $1,132 per share, a 23.9 percent premium to the October 28 close, and an enterprise value of $115 billion. After closing, Marvell holders will own about 67 percent of the combined company and Lumentum holders about 33 percent. Marvell chief executive Matt Murphy stays on as chairman and chief executive, and three Lumentum directors, including its chief executive Michael Hurlston, join Marvell's board. The companies expect to close in the first half of 2028, subject to shareholder votes and regulatory approvals. They cite more than $1 billion of annual run-rate cost synergies, expect the deal to add to Marvell's non-GAAP earnings per share in the first year, and describe a combined addressable market of $550 billion.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The stated logic is physical. As AI clusters grow, copper links run out of bandwidth and reach, so the industry is shifting toward optics, first between buildings and racks and later inside a single rack or package. The companies argue that this shift rewards joint design of electronics and optics rather than buying discrete parts. Putting lasers, silicon photonics, packaging and custom silicon under one roof is meant to let customers buy pre-validated optical solutions faster. For AI researchers the deal is a signal that interconnect, not only compute, is treated as a strategic constraint on scaling. The all-stock structure also means the price moves with an AI-infrastructure equity market that has been volatile, so the headline value could change before closing.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: The long timeline, about 18 months, leaves room for antitrust review, especially in the United States and China, and for shifts in AI spending. Watch for rival optics deals and the joint proxy statement, which will disclose the negotiation history.

papers.title: Latent Reasoning in Continuous Space for Unified Multimodal Models
papers.tldr: LARC lets a unified image model think in continuous hidden states instead of text before drawing, trained with a curriculum and a self-supervised information-gain reward, and it improves with more thinking.
papers.why_selected: Brings latent-space test-time scaling to image generation, with large benchmark gains over its BAGEL base and a clean ablation of the reasoning space.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Unified multimodal models, which both understand and generate images, are meant to benefit from the chain-of-thought tricks that helped language models. In practice, reasoning before drawing often disappoints: more thinking does not reliably give better images, and the controllability seen in language models does not carry over.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Current reasoning-augmented models write their plan as text tokens and then hand it to the image generator. The authors argue this is a modality mismatch. Reasoning passes through a discrete vocabulary, while the image module works with continuous features, so fine-grained spatial information is squeezed out at the token boundary.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: LARC, short for Latent Reasoning in Continuous space, lets the model alternate between writing text and emitting continuous reasoning steps. When the model produces a special latent token, its last-layer hidden state is fed straight back in as the next input embedding, skipping text decoding, in the style of the earlier Coconut method. Training has two stages. First, curriculum supervised fine-tuning starts from text-only reasoning and activates latent steps one at a time, so each new latent builds on a stable prefix; the data are 1 million interleaved reasoning samples, and no latent has an explicit target. Second, reinforcement learning with GRPO uses an information-gain reward: how much the latent trace lowers the image module's flow-matching loss, measured with shared noise, compared with no trace. A penalty on cosine similarity between latents prevents them collapsing into copies.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Built on BAGEL, LARC gains 7 points on GenEval over the base model, with the largest jump, 15 points, on attribute binding. It adds 5.8 percent on DPG-Bench and 10.2 points on OneIG-Bench, and also improves editing. Reinforcement learning lifts GenEval from 0.83 to 0.88 and the visual-reasoning benchmark MIRA from 9.7 to 11.7. Switching from token to latent reasoning from the same base adds 2.6 on MIRA. Performance rises steadily with the latent budget and beats best-of-N sampling at matched compute.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: This is evidence that test-time scaling can work for generation when the reasoning stays in the generator's own representation. The main caveats are that most metrics are model-judged, only one base model was trained, and latent steps are harder to inspect than text plans.

papers.title: Hierarchical World Models with Implicit Dynamics
papers.tldr: ID-WM plans long tasks by using diffusion noise as an abstract action that picks reachable subgoals, while a second model converts each hop into precise actions.
papers.why_selected: Addresses the central weakness of world-model planning, long horizons, with a simple split between where to go and how to get there; strong attention and notable authors.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: A world model predicts what happens after an action, so an agent can plan toward goals it never trained on. But the search space grows exponentially with the number of steps, and small prediction errors compound. Most world-model planners therefore stay short-horizon.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Hierarchical methods split a task into subgoals, but they usually rely on pre-trained skills, fixed macro-actions, value functions or rewards to keep subgoals realistic. That ties them to particular tasks. Without such anchors, a strong optimizer exploits flaws in a learned model and finds unrealistic shortcuts, which the authors call wormholes.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: ID-WM, for Implicit Dynamics World Models, separates reachability from control. A high-level diffusion model takes the current state and a distance, and generates states reachable within that many steps. Its starting Gaussian noise vector is treated as the high-level action, so the planner searches over a smooth, well-behaved unit Gaussian instead of a jagged skill space. A low-level transformer world model then works as an inverse-dynamics solver, finding the actions that carry the agent between consecutive subgoals. Think of choosing waypoints on a map from a generator that only proposes plausible next stops, then letting a driver handle the road. The two levels are optimized together: five subgoals per plan, each 25 environment steps apart, with replanning after every executed plan, up to 15 times.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: On three suites, Wall, PushT and Maze, with horizons up to 2,000 steps, ID-WM improves 38.5 percent overall over baselines that include goal-conditioned imitation, offline reinforcement learning, Diffuser and a hierarchical Diffuser, and 135 percent over a single-level world model with model-predictive control. On PushT with random goals it is the only method above 30 percent success without data augmentation. It also beats an earlier hierarchical world model, HWM, and produces diverse plans, such as rotating the T-block either way.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: It shows hierarchy can come from the generative model's own latent space rather than hand-built skills. The caveats are small simulated environments, three seeds, and only limited visual tests.

papers.title: CaPtain: A Pipeline for Post-Training Code-as-Policy Robot Agents
papers.tldr: CaPtain turns a 4B open vision-language model, which initially solves nothing, into a robot agent that writes code against low-level primitives, using synthetic supervision and reinforcement learning with a simulator-informed critic.
papers.why_selected: Applies the standard agent recipe, supervised fine-tuning then multi-turn reinforcement learning, to physical manipulation, with open weights and strong held-out and zero-shot results.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Code-as-policy robots let a language model write programs that call perception and motion functions. It works impressively with frontier models, but those are costly per episode and cannot run onboard or be fine-tuned.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Prior systems either prompt closed frontier models, or hand the actual grasping to pre-trained vision-language-action models and skill libraries, so the language model only sequences them and is bounded by the skills' training data. Small open vision-language models fail outright when asked to control the robot directly.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: CaPtain gives a small model the full agent recipe with no skills. Its harness exposes 22 low-level capabilities, including segmentation, pointing, geometry measurement and guarded Cartesian moves, in a persistent Python session. There are no grasp or place functions, so the model decides where to grasp, from which direction to approach and when to close the gripper. Each call returns a text receipt of what physically happened. Training first fine-tunes on synthetic trajectories generated by a frontier model, then runs multi-turn reinforcement learning. The difficulty is credit: tens of requests, with effects that appear later, share one end-of-episode outcome. The fix is a physical critic that reads privileged simulator state the policy never sees, and credits each request by how much it changes the predicted chance of success.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Starting from Qwen3.5-4B at 0 percent zero-shot, CaPtain-4B reaches 55.4 percent on held-out LIBERO after fine-tuning and 73.8 percent after reinforcement learning. On LIBERO-PRO it reaches 78.5 percent, above several frontier-model agents, and the reinforcement gains hold across three perturbation suites, by 17.6 to 21.2 points. Without target-domain training it scores 83.3 percent on SimplerEnv WidowX, and it runs on a real robot after simulation-only adaptation. Code, data and weights are released.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The result suggests robot skill can be trained into the language model itself. Limits: reinforcement learning used only 40 LIBERO tasks and one arm, the critic needs simulator state, so online training on hardware would need a state estimator, and force-controlled tasks like wiping are out of reach.

papers.title: Chronos-2: A foundation model for multivariate time series forecasting
papers.tldr: Chronos-2 is a 120M-parameter zero-shot forecaster that uses group attention to learn relationships among related series and covariates in context, trained only on synthetic multivariate data.
papers.why_selected: Shows that in-context learning can carry over to multivariate forecasting with covariates, with large speed advantages and scientific case studies; an extended version of last year's report.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Forecasting underpins epidemiology, economics, energy and hydrology, yet each application usually gets its own model, trained and tuned separately. Real systems are coupled, so a river's flow depends on rainfall and a regional outbreak on neighbouring regions.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Time series foundation models can forecast unseen datasets zero-shot, but most treat every series in isolation, discarding interactions and external drivers. A few earlier attempts at multivariate pretraining had not shown effective zero-shot forecasting with covariates.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: Chronos-2 turns forecasting into in-context learning. Targets and covariates are normalized and cut into patch tokens in one shared space. The transformer alternates two kinds of attention layer. Time attention mixes information along each series. Group attention mixes information across a user-defined group of related series at the same time index, so the model infers dependencies from the history you provide. The same model can run univariate or multivariate depending on how you group inputs. Because real multivariate data with known dependencies is scarce, pretraining uses synthetic data: univariate generators, such as Gaussian-process samples, are combined through random transformations that create instantaneous and lagged relationships. Training uses a quantile loss to give probabilistic forecasts.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: On the fev-bench suite, Chronos-2 improves the point-forecast skill score by 5.2 percentage points over the strongest foundation model baseline and by 11.8 over the best task-specific model, and raises win rate by about 10 points. It also leads on Chronos-Bench-II and GIFT-Eval, which are mostly univariate. It forecasts 100 series in 0.8 seconds on a mid-range GPU, about 50 times faster than the best task-specific point forecaster and 1000 times faster than the best probabilistic one. In case studies on infectious disease, macroeconomics, carbon flux and runoff it often matches or beats specialized methods.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: A small model that adapts at inference time could replace many per-dataset pipelines. The caveat is that the case-study claims are mixed, not uniform wins, and the synthetic prior limits which dependencies the model can recognize.

papers.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
papers.tldr: ACCT converts a small model's already-computed context cache into a compressed cache that a larger model in the same family can use directly, skipping the large model's expensive prefill.
papers.why_selected: Practical idea for multi-model serving with a large speedup, tested across three model families; modest attention but clear deployment relevance.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Serving systems increasingly route requests among models of different sizes. Whenever a new model takes over a conversation or document, it must re-read the entire context, a step called prefill, which is expensive for long inputs.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Prompt caching reuses attention states only within the same model. Token-selection methods such as H2O and SnapKV shrink the cache but stay inside one model. Cache-to-Cache work fuses information across models but still relies on the target's own prefill, and DroidSpeak needs identical architectures. None directly lets a model of a different scale skip reading the context.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: ACCT, for Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer, learns a small transfer interface that turns the source model's hidden states into a sparse key-value cache for the target. Think of a colleague handing over briefing notes written in your own shorthand. Three parts do the work. The Cartographer scores each context token for every target layer and key-value head, using the source states, the query, and the token's position. The Allocator learns how many tokens each head keeps under a shared total budget, because different heads need different amounts of context. The Compiler converts only the selected source representations into target-readable keys and values, keeping original positions. The target then processes just the query. Only the interface is trained, on a single dataset, SearchQA; both models stay frozen.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: The authors test six directed settings across Qwen3 4B and 8B, Llama 3.2 3B and 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B and 32B, on five general benchmarks and six context-dependent tasks. ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's own full-context performance even when cutting the cache by 75 percent. At about 19,000 tokens of context, converting the cache is 6.5 to 21.2 times faster than the target's prefill. Gains on tasks such as TriviaQA, MMLU and PubMedQA show transfer beyond the training dataset.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: It could make routing between small and large models cheaper, with the large model skipping context reading. Caveats: it needs models with shared tokenizers from one family, results vary on multi-hop and language-modeling tasks, and the evaluation sets are small.
